title: Leading a Highly Emotional Colleague
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article offers practical guidance for managing team members who respond intensely to setbacks or disagreements. Rather than trying to change how these colleagues are wired, the author lays out three rules: label the emotion being expressed to lessen its intensity, avoid substantive conversation while emotions are running high and instead pause and revisit later, and, if a pause doesn't help, ask the person to put their views in writing to create productive distance from the emotional charge. The piece frames emotional expression as carrying a kind of honesty that, while uncomfortable, shouldn't be dismissed or suppressed.
points: Highly emotional team members are often wired differently and shouldn't be treated as a problem to fix, as long as they aren't disruptive.
Rule one: label the emotion out loud ("I can see you're frustrated") to lessen its intensity.
Rule two: avoid substantive discussion while emotions run high; pause and revisit the issue later without ending the conversation entirely.
Rule three: if a pause doesn't help, ask the team member to put their views in writing to create distance from the emotional charge.
quotes: these colleagues seem hard-wired to respond intensely to all kinds of situations that wouldn’t bother many others.
Good leaders don’t try to “fix” or change emotional team members.
Scads of research confirm that giving emotions a label lessens their intensity.
High emotionality clouds judgment, slows down decision-making, and amplifies opinions and viewpoints.
Good leaders remember there is a genuine honesty in emotions that is as refreshing as it is uncomfortable at times.
